Learning Objectives
Define adhesive capsulitis.
Identify risk factors for, the etiology of, and the epidemiology of adhesive capsulitis.
Perform an appropriate workup for adhesive capsulitis, including a patient history, physical
examination, and imaging studies.
Review the details of nonsurgical and surgical management of adhesive capsulitis and the
appropriate time frame for each treatment option.

According to the consensus definition of the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons, adhesive
capsulitis is “a condition characterized by functional restriction of both active and passive
shoulder motion for which radiographs of the glenohumeral joint are essentially
unremarkable.”1
Epidemiology
Affects 2% to 5% of the general population2,3
Women more commonly affected than men
Typical age range is 40 to 60 years
Increased prevalence in patients with diabetes mellitus
13% to 20% of patients with diabetes mellitus may experience adhesive capsulitis
Correlation with human leukocyte antigen B27 positivity

American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 771-775.)
Epidemiology

Epidemiology
Primary adhesive capsulitis is considered a self-limiting idiopathic inflammatory and
fibrotic disease of the shoulder, with an incidence of 3% to 5% in the general population.
It classically effects women in their forties and fifties and is considerably more common
in individuals with diabetes mellitus. It is bilateral in as many as 50% of patients and
more often involves the nondominant arm. The disease involves inflammation and
contracture of the shoulder capsule structures and leads to pain and a considerable
decrease in shoulder range of motion (ROM) and function.
Natural History
The onset of symptoms often is idiopathic and insidious but occasionally is related to mild
trauma or change in activity level and medical comorbidities. Secondary adhesive capsulitis
(eg, from surgical management or trauma) also needs to be addressed. 2-4
Adhesive capsulitis has four described clinical stages that differ according to symptomatology
and histologic analyses. Clinical stages are suggested but not definitive. Considerable time
overlap exists between the proposed stages.
Stage 1: the freezing or pre-adhesive stage
Characterized primarily by severe inflammatory pain, especially at night
Typically lasts 10 to 36 weeks
Results in limitations in functional ranges of movement
Stage 2: the frozen or acute adhesive stage
Associated with profound capsular stiffness and limited ROM

Primarily characterized by pain and increasing stiffness with the transition from synovitis to
increasing fibrotic capsular changes
Duration often ranges from 3 to 12 months
Stage 3: the thawing or maturation stage
Drawn out and characterized by slow resolution of symptoms
Inflammation begins to resolve, but the stiffness is initially profound, followed by a slow
and gradual improvement that may last 1 to 3 years.
Because of the decrease in pain, most patients are able to better tolerate shoulder capsule
stretching exercises in stage 3.
Stage 4: the chronic stage
A gradual resolution of symptoms can occur spontaneously or with minimal management
over a period of 6 months to 3 years.
A prolonged recovery or residual symptoms is not uncommon.
A prolonged stage 4 or chronic stage characterized by little or no pain, except if the arm is
suddenly moved to its limited end ROM, has been described.
The natural progression is classically described as self-resolving; however, 20% to 50% of
patients have persistent long-term pain and motion deficits for more than 3 years.2
Risk Factors
Greatest risk factor is a previous diagnosis of adhesive capsulitis in the contralateral shoulder2-
5
Sex: females more commonly affected than males
Diabetes mellitus (types 1 and 2)

Risk Factors
Studies have estimated the prevalence of adhesive capsulitis in individuals with diabetes
mellitus to range from 13% to 20% compared with estimates in the general population of
2% to 5%. Increasing duration and increased severity of diabetes mellitus is associated
with an increased risk for adhesive capsulitis. In addition, males and patients with
diabetes mellitus do not respond as well to treatment for adhesive capsulitis as females
and patients without diabetes mellitus.
Thyroid disease, cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular accidents

Posttraumatic setting
Other associated conditions include mastectomy or lumpectomy, prior chest wall
surgery, and Dupuytren contracture.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Onset: usually described as insidious
Pain
Precedes loss of motion
Worse at extremes of motion
Occurs at night
External rotation: first motion affected
Limitations in activities of daily living
Night pain
Medical history, including risk factor analysis
Physical Examination
Adhesive capsulitis primarily is a clinical diagnosis.
Inspection
Muscle disuse atrophy/asymmetry between shoulders
Previous surgical scars
Palpation
Tenderness at the deltoid insertion and the anterior and posterior capsule
ROM testing
Both sides are compared in forward elevation, abduction, internal and external rotation, and
internal and external rotation at 90° of abduction.
Global loss of active and passive glenohumeral joint motion
Passive and active external rotation typically are the first motions compromised compared
with the contralateral shoulder.
Findings of rotator cuff strength testing usually are normal.

Examination according to stage of disease
Stage 1: painful without considerable loss of motion; onset of pain is noticed before the
capsule limits passive motion.
Stage 2: painful loss of ROM in which the pain worsens with the limits of passive motion
Stage 3: loss of movement in which stiffness predominates; the patient can tolerate capsular
stretching with minimal pain

Physical Examination
The patient history is important to identify key risk factors and rule out other potential
causes of shoulder pain, such as trauma, infection, tumor, or cervical spine pathology.
Patients initially report an insidious onset of shoulder pain and usually night pain,
followed by a decrease in active and passive ROM. External rotation commonly is the
first motion limited. In the early stages, a firm end point may not be noted on physical
examination, and pain will predominate. Eventually, a firm capsular end point to motion
will be apparent on physical examination. The clinician must compare motion and
function of the affected shoulder with that of the unaffected shoulder.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Shoulder radiographs should be obtained to rule out other diagnoses, including glenohumeral
joint osteoarthritis, glenohumeral joint fracture/dislocation, bony neoplasm, and calcific
tendinitis.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Neither MRI nor magnetic resonance angiography is necessary for diagnosis; however, they
may reveal specific findings suggestive of adhesive capsulitis (Figure 4).

Static imaging: thickening of joint capsule, rotator interval, and CHL
Dynamic imaging: shows limited sliding motion of the supraspinatus

Ultrasonography
In general, adhesive capsulitis is a clinical diagnosis and imaging studies are not
required; however, imaging studies may be used as a diagnostic adjunct, to rule out
other pathology, or in ambiguous circumstances. Advanced imaging studies, including
MRI, magnetic resonance angiography, and ultrasonography, primarily focus on
thickening of capsular structures, specifically the CHL and the rotator interval, and
contraction of capsular spaces, including the glenohumeral joint volume and the axillary
fold. Ultrasonography provides dynamic and static imaging studies. An ultrasonographic

11/26

cutoff value greater than 0.7 mm with regard to CHL thickness is associated with a
specificity and sensitivity higher than 90% with regard to the diagnosis of adhesive
capsulitis.2
Pathology
Primarily an inflammatory and fibrotic disorder
Elevated inflammatory cytokines and inflammatory cells in capsular and rotator interval
tissues compared with control tissues

Pathology
In pathologic terms, the disease currently is understood to begin as an inflammatory
disorder that becomes progressively fibrotic, resulting in capsular contraction. A host of
inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor
alpha, transforming growth factor beta, cyclooxygenase 1 and cyclooxygenase 2, make
up the adhesive capsulitis environment, especially during the earlier stages. Samples of
rotator interval tissue consistently contain inflammatory cell types, such as lymphocytes,
macrophages, and mast cells. Histologic specimens of the CHL from patients with
adhesive capsulitis reveal fibroblasts and myofibroblast differentiation, with increased
levels of type 1 and type 3 collagen, consistent with a progressively fibrotic process.
Diagnosis
Primary adhesive capsulitis has an idiopathic etiology with no apparent inciting event.
Secondary adhesive capsulitis often has the same clinical examination findings as primary
adhesive capsulitis; however, secondary adhesive capsulitis occurs after recent surgery or a
traumatic event, such as a proximal humerus fracture or correlated risk factors.
Differential Diagnosis
Glenohumeral arthritis

AAOS | Shoulder Stiffness: Adhesive Capsulitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004056
12/26

Glenohumeral joint fracture or dislocation
Bicipital tenosynovitis
Cervical radiculopathy
Rotator cuff disease, including rotator cuff tear, tendonitis, or calcific tendinitis

Differential Diagnosis
Primary idiopathic adhesive capsulitis is clinical diagnosis and often is a diagnosis of
exclusion. Because shoulder stiffness may be caused by various conditions, other
reasons for shoulder stiffness, including advanced arthritis or advanced rotator cuff
pathology, must be ruled out. Secondary causes of adhesive capsulitis, including those
that occur after traumatic injury or recent surgery, also must be ruled out.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
No contraindications to nonsurgical management exist, and nonsurgical management is the
primary recommended first line of treatment.
Nonsurgical management via a home or physical therapy stretching regimen is universally
accepted as the initial and mainstay treatment option for adhesive capsulitis.
Stretching regimens do not need to be aggressive, and gentle motion is equally as effective.
The literature is inconclusive regarding whether home versus formal therapy programs are
more effective in managing pain and function.

Nonsurgical Management
Because the disease process often is prolonged in duration and has a debilitating effect
on daily function, adjuvant therapies typically are used in combination with physical
therapy or home stretching to improve symptoms and attempt to expedite the course of
the disease. Pharmacologic therapies targeting the inflammatory cascade, including
NSAIDs, oral corticosteroids, and intra-articular corticosteroid injections, have been used
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:33 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Stiffness: Adhesive Capsulitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004056
13/26

to target the inflammatory process of the disease. NSAIDs and oral corticosteroids have
not been shown to offer any lasting advantages; however, their use is aimed at relieving
pain and improving the patient’s ability to participate in the recommended stretching.
These medications also may have a systemic adverse effect profile that must be
considered, including headache, nausea, hypertension, renal and gastrointestinal
complications, and hyperglycemia.
Techniques/Procedures
Physical therapy and stretching
Home-directed exercise and structured physical therapy are beneficial and represent the
mainstay of management.
Intense stretching may be poorly tolerated in the early and middle stages of adhesive
capsulitis secondary to pain.
The literature is inconclusive on the advantages of supervised formal therapy versus a home
stretching regimen.
Pharmacologic treatment options: Oral NSAIDs and oral corticosteroids
Both modalities primarily used for short-term pain management with the goal of facilitating
tolerance to motion and stretching
Studies have shown benefits with regard to short-term pain relief, with mixed results in the
literature with regard to improvement in ROM versus placebo and inferior outcomes
compared with intra-articular corticosteroid injection (CSI).6-8
CSIs
Intra-articular CSIs versus placebo injections have been proven to be beneficial with regard
to pain relief and improved clinical outcomes in multiple prospective randomized studies
with short-term follow-up. Most studies show no long-term advantage if both groups also
undergo standard rehabilitation and stretching techniques.8-12
Intra-articular CSIs have been shown to be more beneficial with regard to pain relief and
improvement in motion than oral steroids or NSAIDs in prospective randomized trials at
short-term follow-up, with one study reporting benefits for as long as a follow-up of 12
months.6-8
Similar advantages have been shown with subacromial and intra-articular CSIs in prospective
randomized trials, with no overall difference in pain relief or functional outcomes; however,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004056
14/26

more rapid pain relief may result from intra-articular injections.12-14
Intra-articular hydrodilatation
Aims to release capsular contracture via intraarticular injection of large amounts of fluid
(often saline and corticosteroids) into the glenohumeral joint to expand capsular volume
A randomized controlled trial demonstrated that hydrodilatation in combination with home
stretching exercises versus subacromial or intra-articular CSI alone results in improved short-
term outcomes (1- and 3-month follow-up) with no difference in long-term outcomes.13
A prospective trial on hydrodilatation versus manipulation under anesthesia alone in
patients with stage 2 disease demonstrated improved visual analog scale and Constant
assessment scores favoring the hydrodilatation group at 6-month follow-up, with no
substantial difference in ROM improvement.15
Suprascapular nerve block (SSNB)
The suprascapular nerve supplies sensory innervation to approximately 70% of the
glenohumeral joint. Limited evidence suggests SSNB results in improved patient ability to
tolerate a stretching regimen with subsequent improved ROM and pain scores.16,17
Evidence suggests that a SSNB in addition to an intra-articular CSI versus intra-articular
injection alone may reliably result in superior short-term improvements in pain and ROM,
with one study showing greater improvement beyond 1 year.18
Future nonsurgical therapies
Collagenases: enzymatic capsulotomy
Clostridium histolyticum collagenase enzyme
Trials currently underway on extra-articular anterior shoulder collagenase injections show
promising results.19
Nonsurgical management compared with surgical management: insufficient evidence to
recommend surgical management as the first-line treatment option for adhesive capsulitis

Techniques/Procedures
CSIs in the glenohumeral joint or the subacromial space have been shown to be effective
in managing pain and improving short-term outcomes compared with placebo or
systemic pharmacologic management. Multiple studies have shown improvement in
objective measures, including ROM and shoulder outcome scores, and improved visual
analog scale pain scores in the short term compared with those for oral corticosteroids
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:33 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Stiffness: Adhesive Capsulitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004056
15/26

or other pharmacological treatment options.6-11 CSIs are as effective as physical therapy
alone with regard to long-term outcomes; however, studies have demonstrated
improved short-term pain and disability scores with CSIs alone and CSIs with physical
therapy compared with physical alone and sham injections.9,10 The most common
adverse effects associated with CSIs are a transient flushing reaction and temporary
hyperglycemia.
Additional, but less commonly used, nonsurgical treatment options include SSNB and
hydrodilatation. SSNB targets the sensory innervation to the glenohumeral joint for pain
control. Combining SSNB with an intra-articular injection results in better improvement
in pain and functional outcomes than that achieved with intra-articular injection alone.18
Hydrodilatation, although commonly categorized as nonsurgical management, is
performed in the operating room with a level of anesthesia similar to that for
manipulation under anesthesia (MUA). During hydrodilatation, the glenohumeral joint is
insufflated with saline until rupture of the capsule is demonstrated by a sudden
decrease in resistance or fluid extravasation observed on fluoroscopy.
Insufficient evidence exists to support surgical management as a first-line treatment
option because most patients with adhesive capsulitis improve over a period of 6 to 18
months. In addition, adjuvant treatment options, including CSI, improve symptoms in the
short term and make the disease course more tolerable. If performed earlier in the
disease process, CSI and surgical treatment options more substantially affect early
outcome measures. Nonsurgical adjuvant treatment options often improve short-term
outcomes; however, little evidence exists to suggest they alter long-term outcomes. This
suggests that although the disease is considered self-limiting, the disease course can be
prolonged. Regardless, studies have shown that 20% to 50% of patients may have long-
term deficits in pain and ROM with nonsurgical treatment alone compared with the
contralateral arm.2,20 Patients who desire to have improved pain and function sooner
elect to undergo more aggressive surgical management if nonsurgical adjuvant therapies
do not provide the desired results.
Surgical Management

Indications
Indications for surgical management include persistent pain and/or failure to show
improvements in ROM after 6 to 12 months of nonsurgical management.
Contraindications
Unwillingness or inability to undergo general anesthesia for medical reasons
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
The clinician should plan to document preoperative ROM in the operating room after the
patient is under anesthesia for comparison with postoperative ROM.
Patients should be placed in the beach-chair or supine position for MUA or arthroscopic
release.
Surgical Approaches
MUA
Manipulation has been shown to be a beneficial method to safely improve ROM and function
in patients in whom initial nonsurgical treatment fails; however, isolated MUA appears to
have a minimal role in patients with adhesive capsulitis.
The Codman paradox technique for MUA (Video 2)
Manipulation should not be performed as an isolated procedure for posttraumatic,
postoperative, and severe cases of adhesive capsulitis secondary to risk of humerus fracture.
The goal of hydrodilatation is to release capsular contracture via intra-articular injection of
large amounts of fluid (often saline and corticosteroids) into the glenohumeral joint to
expand capsular volume.
Studies suggest that compared with CSI alone, hydrodilatation results in improved short-
term outcomes and equivocal long-term outcomes.

Arthroscopic capsule release (ACR) (Video 1)
Risk factors for requiring surgical release include younger age, more severe restriction of
ROM, and failure to show improvement with initial nonsurgical management.
Capsular release can be performed to the 5-o’clock to 7-o’clock positions, with gentle
manipulation performed to address the remaining inferior capsule.
Key anatomic targets for release include the rotator interval tissue, CHL, and anteroinferior
capsule.
Additional release of the posterior capsule (pancapsular) is performed in patients with
restricted internal rotation.
Better early improvement in ROM has been shown after pancapsular release compared
with selective capsule release; however, differences are not maintained in the long term.
Release of scapulohumeral adhesions within the subacromial and subdeltoid space
should be performed before manipulation is attempted in patients with posttraumatic
and postoperative adhesive capsulitis.

Open capsule release
Currently, open release rarely is performed because of advances in arthroscopy.
Open release may be indicated in patients in whom hardware removal may be required
and/or patients with severe posttraumatic or postoperative stiffness.
Open release often is limited by the need for takedown of the subscapularis tendon to
adequately access the joint capsule.
Postoperative Management
These postoperative management measures apply regardless of surgical treatment option
selected.
Postoperative protocols vary; however, in general, a sling may be used for comfort for a
maximum of 1 week postoperatively.
A postoperative interscalene nerve block improves tolerance of early physical therapy and
stretching.
A physical therapy or stretching regimen should begin on postoperative day one.


Postoperative Management
Surgical management for adhesive capsulitis is reserved for refractory cases that do not
respond to a trial of nonsurgical management for 6 to 12 months. Surgical treatment
options include MUA, hydrodilatation, and ACR. As an initial treatment option, MUA
alone offers no clear advantage over physical therapy, self-directed stretching, or steroid
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:33 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Stiffness: Adhesive Capsulitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004056
21/26

injections. Historically, MUA has been safely performed, with beneficial results in
improving long-term ROM; however, it is associated with a risk of fracture, capsulolabral
injury, and painful hemarthrosis. Hydrodilatation has shown promising results in
refractory cases with regard to short-term improvement in pain and function. A single
prospective randomized controlled trial on hydrodilatation in combination with
corticosteroids showed improved early ROM and pain scores at 1 and 3 months
compared with intra-articular or subacromial CSI; however, no difference was noted at 6
months.13 A Cochrane review of five clinical trials concluded that hydrodilatation in
combination with corticosteroids and saline may improve short-term disability pain
compared with a placebo but may not be better than CSI alone.21
The mainstay of modern surgical management is ACR, which results in reproducible
long-term improvement in patient function and pain relief. ACR is an effective and safe
method for the management of recalcitrant disease. Multiple studies have shown short
and long-term improvement in pain and functional outcomes at a mean follow-up of
longer than 7 years, with motion of the injured shoulder being comparable with that of
the contralateral shoulder.22,23 Slower and less overall improvement in pain, function,
and satisfaction often is observed after ACR in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and
postoperative adhesive capsulitis compared with patients who have idiopathic and
posttraumatic adhesive capsulitis.23,24 Complications are rare but include the general
risks associated with arthroscopic shoulder procedures, including infection,
neurovascular injury, and risks associated with anesthesia.
The general goal after ACR is pain control to facilitate ROM exercises as soon as possible.
Most postoperative protocols for adhesive capsulitis include a short period of
immobilization in a sling (1 to 3 days postoperatively), followed quickly by a formal
physical therapy or home stretching protocol to limit the re-establishment of adhesions
and accompanying stiffness. Intraoperative documented ROM should be used to guide
physical therapy goals.
